newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: New UN arms chief worried about Iraq's germ weapons.
newsitem.headline: New UN arms chief worried about Iraq's germ weapons.

text.p: Richard Butler, the Australian U.N. official in charge of ridding Iraq of dangerous weapons, said on Tuesday he would visit Baghdad for the first time this month and expressed particular concern about the country's germ warfare capability.

Butler, during his first day on the job as executive chairman of the U.N. Special Commission (UNSCOM), in charge of scrapping Iraq's weapons of mass destruction, also told Reuters in an interview he was somewhat surprised at the "quantity and quality" of Iraq's overall arsenal.
He said he had spoken to Iraq's deputy prime minister, Tareq Aziz, only a few days ago and set up the trip to Iraq for the last week of July.
"We agreed that in addition to my seeing the (U.N.) operation there and getting acquainted with the good people doing the work, we would have talks of substance," he said.

Butler, 54, a former Australian U.N. ambassador known for his articulate and blunt comments, has been involved in disarmament affairs for 25 years. He replaced Rolf Ekeus, who built UNSCOM in 1991 and will now become Sweden's ambassador in Washington.

A clean bill of health from the commission is a key requirement before the embargo on Iraqi oil exports can be lifted entirely. Iraq has been under U.N. Security Council sanctions since its invasion of Kuwait in August 1990.

Asked, in light of his experience, if he were surprised at anything he found in the commission's files, he replied: "A little, the quantity and quality of weapons involved," which were "sadly large and various."
"But that just made me think even more strongly that 'My God, this job is worth doing,'" he said.
"If I wake up one morning and find I am unemployed because we have finished this job, I am not going to be unhappy about that," he added.

Butler said he was particularly worried about biological weapons, athough there had been varying degrees of progress "or lack of it" in the areas of chemical weapons and ballistic missile technology also.
"Biology though is a big concern at the present time," he said. "The programme as far as we can see has not been small."

"In the hideous world of weapons of mass destruction, the biological stuff is just awful. This is the sort of thing that can kill tens of thousands of people with one bomb, one missile. They are illegal. So, of course they are a matter of concern," Butler said.

Ekeus last month said that when U.N. inspectors visited a university where professors were known to have been involved in a biological weapons programme, one of them tried to escape with a batch of papers.
He was intercepted and the documents were found to relate to "very sensitive development and production efforts concerning a major biological warfare agent, which was not declared before by Iraq."

Iraq recently balked at spot arms inspections, saying the Commission was intruding on sensitive sites. This prompted the Security Council to threaten further sanctions in several months if the situation did not improve.
Butler said that, after speaking to Aziz, "the chances are that there can be a renewed sense of purpose here and we might be able to move forward."
Asked if he would have an easier time on the inspections, he said, "I am not so young and foolish as to make such predictions."

"But rest assured," he warned, "that when there are actions such as those that occurred a few weeks ago, the chairman of UNSCOM must report them to the Security Council. There was nothing personal about it."
"I emphasised to him (Aziz) that this is a scientific and technical and objective job. With Iraq's cooperation we can do it," he said.

"But I want to make this very clear. My job is not to decide the politics or the policies of the Security Council," he added. "My job and those of the other staff in the Commission is to go and look for weapons of mass destruction, to identify them, to verify them....to get rid of them."
"The technologies that I am responsible for should drive the politics, not the politics the technology," he added.
